--- title: "Balance Theory and Signed Graphs" subtitle: "The Structure and Dynamics of Valenced Networks" format: revealjs: scrollable: true theme: default center: false css: ucla-theme.css width: 1280 height: 720 margin: 0.1 min-scale: 0.2 --- # Part 1: The Relational Basis of Valenced Networks & Dyadic Balance --- ## Balance Theory and Signed Graphs ### The Local and Global Dynamics of Sentiment Networks ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.incremental} - Relationships are not just present or absent; they carry emotional **valence**. - **Balance Theory** is the foundational framework linking: - Local, psychological micro-motives. - Global, macro-structural network patterns (like polarization). - Today we will cover: Dyadic Balance, Triadic Balance, Structural Balance, Clusterability, and Ranked Clusterability. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ## The Anatomy of Sentiment Networks ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Valenced ties** are links representing positive ($+$) or negative ($-$) feelings, evaluations, or behaviors. - *Positive valence*: Liking, helping, admiring, loving. - *Negative valence*: Hating, bullying, fighting, distrusting. - A **signed graph** features a set of vertices $V$ and two disjoint sets of edges: - Positive links ($E^+$) and negative links ($E^-$). - These networks represent stable social attitudes rather than fleeting events. - We can represent them with a **signed adjacency matrix**: $+1$ for positive ties, $-1$ for negative ties, $0$ for no tie. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ## Fritz Heider's Dyadic Balance ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Developed by social psychologist **Fritz Heider** (1946) to examine how ties cohere within a single pair. - Distinction between: - **Symmetric ties**: Relations implied by similarity or co-membership (e.g., sharing a workspace). - **Asymmetric ties**: Directional sentiments (e.g., liking). - **First Proposition**: Similarity breeds liking. Sharing co-membership or space breeds positive asymmetric ties ($aSb \implies aLb$). - Forms a **positive feedback loop**: We spend more time with those we like ($aLb \implies aSb$). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ## Proximity, Similarity, and Multiplexity ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.incremental} - Over time, people accumulate multiple types of ties, leading to **multiplex ties** ("multistranded" connections). - **Principle of Propinquity** (Newcomb 1956): Sharing physical space or social contexts automatically facilitates acquaintance and liking. - Proximity breeds interaction, which breeds similarity, which in turn breeds liking, support, and advice. - Relationships transition from uniplex (single-stranded) to multiplex. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ## Dyadic Balance and Cognitive Tension ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Second Proposition**: We strive to maintain positive asymmetric ties with those we are similar to. - Situations where similarity is paired with dislike ($aSb \land aDb$) are **unbalanced**. - Creates **cognitive inconsistency** and an unpleasant state of **affective tension** (e.g., hating a forced co-worker). - **Resolution of Imbalance**: - Break the similarity tie (e.g., quit the job). - Transform the dislike into liking (e.g., adapt to like the co-worker). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- # Part 2: Triadic Balance Theory --- ## Fritz Heider’s P-O-Q Triad ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - To analyze triads, Heider extended dyadic balance to three distinct elements: the **P-O-Q Triad**. - **Person (P)**: The focal individual from whose cognitive perspective the triad is analyzed. - **Other (O)**: Towards whom P holds a directed sentiment. - **Third Party / Object (Q)**: Another actor, group, organization, or abstract cultural idea. - Sentiments are modeled via **directed, signed edges** ($+$ or $-$) going from P to O, P to Q, and O to Q. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ## The Mathematics of Triadic Balance ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.incremental} - A triad is **balanced** if the product of its three edge signs is positive: $$\text{Sign}(P, O) \times \text{Sign}(O, Q) \times \text{Sign}(P, Q) = +1$$ - **Simplified Identification Rule**: A triad is balanced if it has an **even number of negative links** (exactly zero or two). - Balanced configurations are stable and represent **harmonious sentiments**, creating no cognitive tension. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} | Edge P-O | Edge O-Q | Edge P-Q | Product | State | | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+1$ | **Balanced** | | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+1$ | **Balanced** | | $+$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+1$ | **Balanced** | | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+1$ | **Balanced** | | $+$ | $+$ | $-$ | $-1$ | **Unbalanced** | | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ | $-1$ | **Unbalanced** | | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ | $-1$ | **Unbalanced** | | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-1$ | **Unbalanced** | ::: ::: --- ## Balanced Triads: The 4 Stable Configurations ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.incremental} 1. **"A friend of a friend is a friend"** ($+ \times + \times + = +1$) - *Example*: You (P) and friend (O) both like the same classmate (Q). 2. **"An enemy of an enemy is a friend"** ($- \times - \times + = +1$) - *Example*: You (P) and ally (Q) form a bond against a mutual rival (O). 3. **"A friend of an enemy is an enemy"** ($- \times + \times - = +1$) - *Example*: Your rival (O) has a close friend (Q); you start to dislike Q. 4. **"An enemy of a friend is an enemy"** ($+ \times - \times - = +1$) - *Example*: Your country ally (O) declares war on country (Q); you also oppose Q. :::
::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ## Unbalanced Triads: The 4 Unstable Configurations ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.incremental} 1. **"A friend of my friend is my enemy"** ($+ \times + \times - = -1$) - *Example*: Friend (O) likes (Q), whom you (P) dislike. 2. **"An enemy of a friend is a friend"** ($+ \times - \times + = -1$) - *Example*: Partner (O) hates Marvel movies (Q), which you (P) love. 3. **"A friend of an enemy is a friend"** ($- \times + \times + = -1$) - *Example*: You (P) and your rival (O) are both attracted to the same person (Q). 4. **"An enemy of my enemy is also my enemy"** ($- \times - \times - = -1$) - *Example*: You (P) dislike both the Yankees (O) and Red Sox (Q). :::
::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ## Tension and Change ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.incremental} - Unbalanced configurations produce psychological discomfort, making them **socially unstable**. - This discomfort acts as an **engine of change**, driving social networks to transition toward balanced configurations. - Transition occurs when the focal actor (P) changes the **sign/valence** of their ties to resolve tension. - Balanced configurations, having no tension, are stable **equilibrium states**. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ## Cross-Pressure ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Cross-pressure** (Davis 1963) occurs when an individual experiences conflicting social relations, leaving them caught between opposing forces. - When P is positively tied to O1 and O2 ($+$, $+$), but O1 likes Q and O2 dislikes Q. - According to balance theory, P is forced to develop an **ambivalent attitude** ($+/-$) toward Q. - To resolve this tension, P must either distance themselves from one friend or convince them to reconcile. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ## Cross-Pressure in Real-Life: Politics ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.incremental} - Political preferences provide a classic illustration of cross-pressure. - Imagine you (P) have a brother (O1) who is a passionate Democrat ($+$) and a sister (O2) who strongly opposes them ($-$). - Because you have positive bonds with both, you find yourself cross-pressured regarding the Democrats (Q). - This pressure produces **social ambivalence**, often leading individuals to identify as moderates or **independents** with no strong partisan affiliation. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- # Part 3: Structural Balance Theory & Whole-Network Polarization --- ## Structural Balance at the Network Level ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Balance theory can be scaled up from individual cognitive triads to the **whole network** level. - This extension is known as **Structural Balance Theory**. - In its original formulation, it applies to **complete signed graphs**, where every pair of actors is connected by either a positive or negative link. - In a **signed adjacency matrix** representation of a signed graph: - Positive links are represented by $+1$. - Negative links are represented by $-1$. - Non-adjacent nodes are represented by $0$. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ## The Fundamental Theorem of Structural Balance ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Discovered by mathematicians Dorwin **Cartwright** and Frank **Harary** in 1956. - **Theorem (Cartwright–Harary Structure Theorem)**: A signed graph — *complete or incomplete* — is balanced if and only if its nodes can be partitioned into exactly **two polarized factions** such that: 1. All positive links exist *within* each faction. 2. All negative links exist *between* the two factions. - Shows that structural balance is equivalent to perfect **group polarization**. - For *complete* graphs, the test is simple: a complete signed graph is balanced if and only if **every triad is balanced** (the triad test is the complete-graph shortcut). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ## Signed Matrices & Faction Detection ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.incremental} - How can we mathematically recover and identify factions in a balanced network? - Rearrange the rows and columns of the **signed adjacency matrix** such that nodes in the same faction are adjacent. - This permutation yields a **block-diagonal signed matrix**. - Inside the diagonal blocks, cells are $+1$ (internal cohesion), whereas off-diagonal blocks are entirely $-1$ (external conflict). - The 3 × 3 blocks below mirror the two three-person factions in the previous slide's graph. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ### Faction Block-Diagonal Matrix $$M = \begin{pmatrix} \begin{array}{ccc|ccc} \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & - & - & - \\ \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & - & - & - \\ \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & - & - & - \\ \hline - & - & - & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} \\ - & - & - & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} \\ - & - & - & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} & \mathbf{+} \end{array} \end{pmatrix}$$ ::: ::: --- ## Cycles and Paths in Balanced Graphs ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Partitioning has direct, rigid consequences for paths and cycles in complete graphs: - **Cycles**: *All cycles in a balanced signed graph must have a positive sign product.* - Staying inside a group uses only positive links. - Spanning across groups requires crossing the boundary an *even* number of times, multiplying an even number of negative signs to yield a positive product. - **Paths**: - Paths ending in the *same* group have a **positive product**. - Paths ending in *different* groups have a **negative product** (due to odd boundary crossings). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ## Checking for Balance with Matrix Powers ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - How can we test balance in a large network without drawing every cycle? - Raise the signed adjacency matrix $\mathbf{A}$ to the $p$-th power. - Each diagonal entry $a_{ii}^{(p)}$ sums the sign products of all **closed walks** of length $p$ starting and ending at node $i$. - **The test**: If the graph is balanced, every diagonal entry of $\mathbf{A}^p$ is **non-negative** for all $p$ up to the number of nodes. - A single negative diagonal entry reveals a negative cycle of length $p$ — and the graph is unbalanced. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ### The test in symbols $$a_{ii}^{(p)} \geq 0 \; \text{for all } i,\; p = 1, \dots, g$$ If any entry is negative: $$a_{ii}^{(p)} < 0 \implies \text{unbalanced cycle}$$ - No need to enumerate cycles — the matrix does the counting. - A practical check for real, messy networks. ::: ::: --- ## Measuring Partial Balance ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Real networks are almost never *perfectly* balanced, so we measure the **degree** of balance. - **Cycle Index of Balance**: the share of all cycles whose sign product is positive. $$\text{Cycle Index} = \frac{PC}{TC}$$ - Ranges from 0 (completely unbalanced) to 1 (perfectly balanced). - **Line Index of Balance** (Harary 1959): the minimum number of edge signs that must be flipped to make the graph perfectly balanced. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} - A large network with a Line Index of 1 or 2 is extremely close to complete balance. - Even when cycle-counting finds dozens of unbalanced cycles, a small Line Index says the polarized structure is nearly there. - Short cycles matter more psychologically, so weighted versions (Henley, Horsfall & De Soto 1969) give triads extra weight. ::: ::: --- ## Directed Balance: Semicycles ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Real sentiment ties are often **asymmetric** — you like someone who dislikes you. - Restricting balance to strict **directed cycles** (arrows all pointing the same way) would miss most tension: Your friend Alex dislikes Jordan, yet you like both. No directed cycle exists, but the tension is real. - **Semipath**: a path that *ignores* arrow direction. - **Semicycle**: a closed semipath (a cycle in the underlying undirected graph). - **A signed digraph is balanced** if and only if **every semicycle has a positive sign** (an even number of negative arcs). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} - The Cartwright–Harary partition rule carries over unchanged: positive arcs within factions, negative arcs between them. - One rule-violating positive tie across factions injects unbalanced semicycles into the whole network. - This is the directed version of everything we just did with cycles. ::: ::: --- ## Empirical Case Study: Political Blogs ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.incremental} - Balanced states describe stable **polarization and conflict**, not harmony. - **Adamic & Glance (2005)** examined the hyperlink network of 2004-election political bloggers. - Two highly connected factions (Liberals, Conservatives); dense internal linking, sparse cross-group linking — an **echo chamber**. - The hyperlink data are *unsigned*; the figure's negative ties illustrate the predicted structure, not measured hostility. - Balance explains why polarized factions are **stable** — and a balanced state need not be a "good" one. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- # Part 4: Clusterability and Multi-Group Partitioning --- ## Beyond Two Factions: Davis's Theorem ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Cartwright & Harary's model splits networks into exactly *two* opposing factions. - This is too restrictive for many real-world networks, such as school cliques, gangs, or multi-party politics. - In 1967, sociologist **James Davis** introduced his **Clusterability Theorem**. - He generalized structural balance so that a network could fragment into **any number of distinct clusters** ($k \ge 1$), rather than just two. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ## The All-Negative Triad Rule ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.incremental} - Classical balance considers a triad with three negative ties (everyone hating everyone else) to be *unbalanced*. - Davis argued that in highly factionalized contexts, it is perfectly stable for three individuals from completely different, competing groups to dislike one another. - **The Clustering Criterion (Davis 1967)**: A graph is **clusterable** if and only if it contains **no cycle of any length with exactly one negative tie**. - For *complete* graphs this reduces to a triad test: no triad with exactly one negative tie. All-positive, two-negative, and all-negative triads are all permitted. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ## Ranked Clusterability: Bridging Balance and Hierarchy ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.incremental} - Balance and clusterability both assume *horizontal*, symmetric sentiment structures. - Real groups often have **vertical hierarchies** — status, dominance, prestige. - **Ranked Clusterability** (Davis & Leinhardt 1972): clusters that are themselves *hierarchically ordered*. - **Within clusters**: horizontal, positive ties (peer solidarity). - **Between clusters**: vertical ties. Positive ties point *up* the hierarchy (deference); negative or null ties point down or across unranked clusters. - This is the mathematical bridge from balance theory to status and **dominance hierarchies**. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} - Think of an office: peers are mutual friends, everyone looks up to the executives, discipline flows downward. - Same local logic (no odd cycles of negativity), but the factions are now *stacked*, not side by side. - Coming up next: theories of valenced interactions, including dominance hierarchies in detail. ::: ::: --- ## Summary: Structural Balance vs. Clusterability ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.incremental} - **Structural Balance (Cartwright-Harary 1956)**: - Local rule: Triads cannot have an odd number of negative ties. - Global topology: Splits the network into exactly **two factions**. - **Clusterability (Davis 1967)**: - Local rule: Relaxes constraints by permitting all-negative triads (no triads with exactly one negative tie). - Global topology: Splits the network into **any number of clusters ($k \ge 1$)**. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](balance-signed-graphs_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: :::
